lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, which scale did blues players bend and improvise on? (The blues scale.) Today: the 20th century, when music changed faster than ever.
Claude Debussy (1862-1918) painted moods in sound, sometimes with the whole-tone scale: six notes, each a tone apart, with no home note. In 1913 Igor Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring shocked Paris.
Jazz grew in New Orleans around 1900, from the blues, ragtime, brass bands and African American church music. Louis Armstrong (1901-1971) made the solo the star.
Some composers left keys behind. Arnold Schoenberg (1874-1951) used all 12 notes equally, so no note feels like home. In 1952 John Cage's piece 4 minutes 33 seconds has the players play nothing.
Electronic music: the theremin, from about 1920, is played without being touched. From 1948 Pierre Schaeffer made music from recorded sounds. Synthesisers build sounds from waves.
Minimalism, from the 1960s, repeats short patterns for a long time and changes them slowly. Two loops of different lengths drift apart and meet again: loops of 3 and 4 beats meet every 12 beats.
Worked example: loops of 4 and 6 beats. Count in fours: 4, 8, 12. Count in sixes: 6, 12. Both reach 12, so the loops start together again every 12 beats.
Try it in the world: with a friend, clap a 3-beat pattern while they clap a 4-beat one, starting together. Count until you meet again. Next: jazz and improvising.

exercises.hint: Are all the steps the same size?
exercises.explain: Every step is a whole tone and there are six notes before the top: a whole-tone scale.

exercises.prompt: Match each musician to their music.
exercises.hint: Think back to the lesson's cards.
exercises.explain: Debussy used the whole-tone scale, Stravinsky wrote The Rite of Spring, Armstrong played jazz solos and Cage wrote a silent piece.

exercises.prompt: Jazz began around 1900 in New Orleans.
exercises.explain: True: jazz grew in New Orleans around 1900.

exercises.prompt: Two loops of 3 and 4 beats start together. After how many beats do they start together again?
exercises.hint: Count in threes and in fours until both reach the same number.

exercises.prompt: Listen. What happens in this music?
exercises.hint: Can you hum the pattern after a few goes?
exercises.explain: The same short pattern plays again and again: the heart of minimalism.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Does this melody have a home note?
choices: no: no note feels like home
yes: it clearly ends at home
exercises.hint: Does the ending sound finished and settled?
exercises.explain: It uses all 12 notes equally, so no note feels like home, as in Schoenberg's music.

exercises.prompt: A 6-beat pattern and an 8-beat pattern begin together. After how many beats do they line up again?
exercises.hint: List the counts in sixes and in eights.
exercises.explain: 6, 12, 18, 24 and 8, 16, 24: they line up after 24 beats.
The Rite of Spring (1913), the theremin (about 1920), Schaeffer's recorded sounds (1948), Cage's silence (1952), minimalism (the 1960s).

exercises.hint: Does it make its sound by itself, or with electricity?
exercises.explain: The trumpet and double bass sound by themselves; the theremin, synthesiser and drum machine need electricity.

exercises.prompt: In a whole-tone scale every step is a whole tone.
exercises.explain: True: there are no semitones, so no note feels like home.

exercises.prompt: Listen to the two parts. What happens?
choices: they drift apart, then meet again
exercises.hint: Listen to the start and the very end.
exercises.explain: One loop is 3 notes and the other 4, so they drift apart and start together again after 12 beats.

exercises.prompt: A 5-beat drum loop and a 3-beat bass loop begin together. After how many beats do they line up again?
exercises.hint: Find the first number both counts reach.

exercises.prompt: Why did The Rite of Spring shock its first audience in 1913?
exercises.hint: Think about what was new in it.
exercises.explain: Its pounding, uneven rhythms and clashing chords were unlike anything the audience knew.

exercises.prompt: A theremin player starts on A4, 440 Hz, and slides up an octave. What is the new frequency in Hz?
exercises.hint: What does going up an octave do to a frequency?
exercises.explain: An octave up doubles the frequency: 440 × 2 = 880 Hz.

exercises.prompt: Listen: the two parts play the same pattern, one starting a beat later.
exercises.hint: Listen to the first beat: how many parts play?
exercises.explain: True: the second part enters one beat late with the same notes, so the two patterns interlock.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Is this a whole-tone scale or a major scale?
exercises.explain: It has semitones between E and F and between B and C: a major scale.
